summary.text: A blazar is an active galactic nucleus whose relativistic jet, made of ionized matter at nearly the speed of light, points almost straight at us.
Relativistic beaming makes blazars look much brighter than they would if the jet pointed away from Earth.
Blazars are highly variable, often changing sharply in brightness over hours to days, and they give off gamma ray photons.

facts.label: Two types
facts.value: BL Lac objects and flat-spectrum radio quasars

facts.label: Jet speed
facts.value: Plasma can move at 99.5% of light speed

items.prompt: Two jets are physically identical. One points almost straight at Earth and the other points away. How do they look to us?

options.label: They look equally bright
The one aimed at us looks much brighter
The one aimed away looks brighter
The one aimed at us looks dimmer

items.explain: Beaming makes a jet pointed toward us appear much brighter, while a receding jet appears dimmer.

items.prompt: A black hole launches matching jets in opposite directions. Why does one often look much weaker than the other?

options.label: The weaker one has less powerful plasma
The weaker one is blocked by the galaxy
The weaker one is cooler than the other
The one moving away from us is dimmed by relativistic effects

items.explain: A receding counter-jet appears dimmer because of relativistic beaming, so identical jets can look asymmetric.

items.prompt: One blazar has weak or no emission lines and another has strong ones. What are these two kinds called?

options.label: A BL Lac object and a flat-spectrum radio quasar
A flat-spectrum radio quasar and a BL Lac object
Two BL Lac objects of different power
Two flat-spectrum radio quasars of different age

items.explain: Blazars divide into BL Lac objects, with weak or no emission lines, and flat-spectrum radio quasars, with strong emission lines.

items.prompt: What helps keep a blazar's jet narrow and focused as it travels outward?

options.label: The gravity of stars across the host galaxy
Thick dust packed tightly around the jet
Strong magnetic fields and winds from the disk and toroid
The slow spin of the galaxy's outer arms

items.explain: The jet is collimated by a combination of intense magnetic fields and powerful winds from the accretion disk and toroid.

items.prompt: Dense gas clouds in a ring around a blazar's black hole soak up and re-emit energy. How does an observer on Earth notice them?

options.label: They appear as dark patches in photos
They show up as emission lines in the blazar's spectrum
They dim the jet's gamma rays
They make the jet's speed vary

items.explain: The clouds absorb and re-emit energy and are detected on Earth as emission lines in the blazar spectrum.

items.prompt: In ordinary visible-light photos, a blazar looks like a compact point. What do sharper images show?

options.label: It sits at the center of an elliptical galaxy
It is a lone star in our galaxy
It is a spiral galaxy seen edge-on
It is a gas cloud between galaxies

items.explain: Most blazars look pointlike in visible light, but high-resolution images show they are at the centers of elliptical galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: What a blazar is
paragraphs.text: A blazar is an active galactic nucleus whose relativistic jet, a stream of ionized matter moving at nearly the speed of light, points almost straight at the observer. The name blends BL Lacertae and quasar, and was coined in 1978 by the astronomer Edward Spiegel. Blazars come in two kinds: BL Lac objects, with weak or no emission lines, and flat-spectrum radio quasars, or FSRQ, with strong ones.

paragraphs.heading: Why it looks so bright
paragraphs.text: Relativistic beaming of the jet's radiation makes a blazar look much brighter than it would if the jet pointed away from Earth. Blazars shine strongly across the electromagnetic spectrum and give off high-energy gamma ray photons. Their brightness often swings sharply within hours or days. Some blazar jets even seem to move faster than light, called superluminal motion, another result of matter in the jet rushing toward us at nearly light speed.

paragraphs.heading: The engine at the center
paragraphs.text: Like every active galactic nucleus, a blazar is believed to draw its power from material dropping into a supermassive black hole at the core of its host galaxy. Gas, dust and now and then a star spiral inward, forming a hot accretion disk that releases huge amounts of energy as photons, electrons, positrons and other particles. This region is relatively small, about 10⁻³ parsecs across. Around it lies a larger opaque toroid of hot gas stretching several parsecs, with denser clouds that absorb and re-emit energy. Seen from Earth, those clouds appear as emission lines in the blazar's spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: The jets
paragraphs.text: Two relativistic jets run at right angles to the accretion disk, carrying very energetic plasma away. Strong magnetic fields and powerful winds from the disk and toroid keep each jet narrow. These jets can reach many tens of kiloparsecs from the black hole. In visible-light images most blazars look compact and pointlike, but high-resolution images show they sit at the centers of elliptical galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: How beaming works
paragraphs.text: A simple model links the light a jet gives off in its own frame, Sₑ, to the light seen on Earth, Sₒ. In it, Sₒ is proportional to Sₑ × D², with D standing for the doppler factor. One part of the boost comes from time dilation, which speeds up the apparent release of energy. A jet that sends out a burst every minute in its own frame might be seen from Earth bursting about every ten seconds.

paragraphs.heading: Angle is everything
paragraphs.text: Picture a jet moving at 99.9% of the speed of light, aimed θ = 5° away from our line of sight. From Earth it would look 70 times brighter than the light it emits. Pointed straight at us, at θ = 0°, it would look 600 times brighter. In the same example, a jet at more than 35° looks dimmer from Earth than from its own frame. The opposite jet, moving away from us, looks dimmer for the same reason, so two identical jets appear clearly lopsided.
